attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, not a quotation of someone else.

semantics.note: 'Nobody wants this' is firm, unhedged language about data centers. Reading it as 'essentially no public appetite' keeps the strength of the words and leaves out the separate economics clause.

contract.note: The plain reading allows for exaggeration but holds 'nobody' to meaning negligible support. That is an ordinary reading of firm words. A weaker reading of just 'widespread opposition' would be easier on the speaker than his words allow. The August 1–21 window is reasonable.

evidence.note: National weighted survey of 2,007 adults, fielded Aug 8–12, before the post. 31% support building AI-training data centers and 26% support a local data center. That is a substantial supporting minority, even though opposition is larger.

reviews.rationale: The representative August polling meets the contract's contradiction condition: about three in ten Americans support AI-training data centers, and about a quarter support one locally. Opposition is greater, but support is far from absent, so 'nobody wants this' fails even with an allowance for exaggeration.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. The examples he cites were collected by a pollster, but the summary claim is his.

semantics.note: The rats-and-ships simile is rhetorical, but the core claim, a rapid Republican retreat from data centers, can be tested. Reading 'Republicans' as politicians fits his framing of public opinion 'refracted through politics'.

contract.note: Reading it as a noticeable, rapid retreat rather than unanimity is fair. The Aug 19–21 window follows from his references to Wednesday and the last 24 hours.

evidence.note: Dated reporting: Rogers called for a moratorium on Aug 20, after taking a friendlier position in July. Barrett ran a campaign attack ad and introduced bills, and Abbott promoted his earlier halt, all inside the window.
Barrett's own office confirms the new bills but describes his opposition to subsidies as longstanding, so his case is intensified opposition rather than a reversal.
Trump kept backing data centers on Aug 21. That rules out a party-wide retreat, which the claim did not require.

reviews.rationale: Several prominent Republicans publicly distanced themselves within the window. Rogers changed position, Barrett stepped up his opposition with new bills and an ad, and Abbott promoted restrictions. Trump's continued support and Barrett's longer record narrow the claim but do not overturn it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own summary of the cited estimates.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'really optimistic' qualifier and the unqualified 'Capex in the trillions'.

contract.note: The contract requires realized revenue in a quarter Marcus never named. 'Current revenues' would ordinarily be read as an annual run rate, so this requirement stretches his words. The capex window is also left undefined.

evidence.note: Annualized generative-AI revenue estimates of about $150bn to $220bn for mid-2026. These sit in the low hundreds of billions, but they are run rates, not the realized basis the contract requires.
Published Oct 19, after the post: a projection that 2026 AI capex will approach $1T. It is a forecast, not completed spending, and does not settle the trillions comparison over any defined window.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no realized industry revenue figure for the period and no defined capex window. The annualized estimates fall within the speaker's optimistic range, and the annual capex projection approaches but does not clearly reach trillions. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Might' qualifies the speculation about big tech being screwed. The toxicity of data centers is stated as a premise without hedging. Reading it as political toxicity fits the Part II context.

contract.note: Defining it as substantial public resistance plus political pressure, without requiring universal opposition, is an ordinary reading.

evidence.note: August Heatmap poll of registered voters: 75% oppose a nearby data center, with opposition spanning parties.
Aug 19 reporting: candidates distancing themselves, and Republicans attacking an opponent as 'Data Center David'.
Texas governor's own Aug 13 release setting audit requirements before projects proceed. It shows restrictive political action, though the restrictions are conditional, not a ban.
Ties to tech companies through community funding drew no backlash. That limits the claim at the edges without undercutting the liability from backing development.

reviews.rationale: August polling shows broad cross-party opposition, and contemporaneous reporting and official records show politicians distancing themselves, imposing restrictions, and using data centers as a line of attack. That meets the support condition. Trump's stance and the community-funding point are limits, not contradictions.
